stemBlocks.value: Determine, algebraically, the x-intercept and the y-intercept of the line y = 3x − 1.
Think first: An intercept is where one of the coordinates is zero, so set each coordinate to zero in turn.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p069-q04 from workbook page 69.

solutionSteps.instruction: Set x = 0 to find the y-intercept.
Set y = 0 to find the x-intercept.

strategyBlocks.value: Put x = 0 to find the y-intercept and y = 0 to find the x-intercept, solving the resulting equation each time.

whyThisWorks.value: Every point on the y-axis has x = 0, and every point on the x-axis has y = 0. Substituting those values turns the two-variable equation into a simple one-variable equation whose solution is the missing coordinate. This is why intercepts can always be found without drawing anything.

commonErrors.misconception: Swapping the two substitutions and setting y = 0 to find the y-intercept.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Swapping the two substitutions and setting y = 0 to find the y-intercept.

commonErrors.misconception: Giving the intercepts as single numbers rather than coordinates.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Giving the intercepts as single numbers rather than coordinates.

commonErrors.misconception: Writing x = 3 by dividing the wrong way round in 3x = 1.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing x = 3 by dividing the wrong way round in 3x = 1.

examTip.value: Say it as you write it: on the y-axis x is zero, on the x-axis y is zero. That sentence prevents the most common intercept error.
